title: Three Weeks in Japan: On Travel and the In Between – John Watson
content:
Photos don’t magically appear, and text doesn’t write itself. Not over here at The Radavist, at least. In the era of AI content slop, we pride ourselves on doing things the human way. This includes late nights, sore bodies, and in-depth, world-famous Reportage. During our whirlwind trip in Japan with Sim Works, we managed to stay sane through camaraderie and by absorbing the wonderful culture of the regions we traveled through. Read on for a short but sweet homage to travel and the in-between time that makes these trips so fulfilling, written and documented by John, with fun BTS by Sim Works brand director Masashi Kimura…

Photo Masashi Kimura

Settling into the end-of-year recaps over here at The Radavist, and still coming off a post-travel high from our time in Japan, I couldn’t help but write a reflective post from our three weeks on the road in the land of the rising sun.

I’ve been thinking a lot about the differences between tourism and travel. As someone who has been to Japan a number of times over the past twenty years, I’m very conscious about being a gaijin, or outsider. During our time in Osaka for Bespoked, Cari and I couldn’t help but notice how clueless so many English-speaking foreigners were. Talking loudly on cellphones on the subway, being drunk in public in the middle of the day, ignoring respectful customs at temples, and being disruptive in restaurants. It felt jarring at times.

Photos Masashi Kimura

Tourism like that feels extractive. Travel, however, where you learn customs ahead of time and adapt your behavior to attempt assimilation, can be a wholly immersive experience. A tourist is egocentric, framing their view through self-interest, resulting in placelessness. They attempt to assimilate their surroundings to themselves. Meanwhile, a traveler hopes to gain a deeper understanding of a culture through respectful observation, deepening their understanding of place.

Cari, working early one morning: photo by John; John and Paul working late photo Masashi Kimura

This is why I absolutely adore what we do over here at The Radavist. Traveling to various factories, riding in bike events, and visiting bike shops give you a truly insider’s perspective on a country or locale and its traditions. Sure, my Japanese could always be better, and at 6’2″, I was constantly bumping my head. My physical stature was out of place in a country like Japan, but I tried my hardest to respect the culture as we visited various historical sites, and I will be forever grateful for this trip.

A brief architectural aside: After Bespoked, Cari and I spent a day visiting Tadao Ando’s Nakanoshima Children’s Book Forest, a children’s library perched on the Tosahori River. In an era where books are banned, it felt ceremonial to visit a space by one of the world’s most accomplished architects that celebrated them. Ando gave back to his home city of Osaka by investing in future generations with this project. A 45º circulation ramp intersects the space, bringing you close to books you can touch and away from those meant for display only. The scale was smaller, more intimate, and details were designed for children. 

Road trips with acquaintances often forge lifelong friendships. For over a week, Masashi Kimura drove Cari, Paul from Slow Spin Society, and me around in his wagon, through confusing traffic patterns in Tokyo and navigating streets so tight they required a spotter to squeeze through. On the road, plentiful highway-side konbini stops were made for snacks including onigiri, salty corn chips, Shigekix sour snacks, and the most intense sparkling water I’ve ever had. Each evening for dinner, we sampled local delicacies ranging from world-famous udon to sashimi, tempura, and more.

We all fell into a rhythm that matched our busy itinerary. Every morning began at 6:00 with a loud alarm, meeting at 7:30 in the lobby of whatever cheap hotel we could find, on site at 8 AM. Our shoots were long, with the iPhone Notepad and Google Translate always at the front of our app folder. Each night, returning to our new home for the night, photos were dumped, edited, and cataloged. Backed up on Dropbox and notes culled. I jotted down how I was feeling in that moment, or takeaways and “aha” moments, in hopes of returning to the mindset once we returned home in the States. Rinse. Repeat.

We had a single day of respite in the coastal city of Zushi, where we stopped for coffee multiple times (returning to the same shop), meandered streets off the beaten path, visited temples built by the Samurai, and rubbed the Buddha statue to cure our aching backs. Cari swam, a soothing refresh for a Cancerian living in a dry and arid place who longs for water.

Come the end of our time together with Masashi and Paul, Cari and I couldn’t help but feel like we’d made friends for life. Separated by a 14-hour flight, our newfound family would be reunited at trade shows, and connections maintained through video calls. As important as our newly formed friendship is, there was an even deeper reverence for the Japanese cycling industry. From the factory workers to the bike shop employees at Circles and Blue Lug, and the landscapes we traversed and the kilometers we covered by bicycle.

Blue Lug Kamiuma, photo Masashi Kimura

Being a traveler through this wonderful country is something I’ll never take for granted. These memories will always live on the website, but more importantly, they’re stored in my heart.

To everyone we met along the way on this trip, to MKS, Nitto, and Honjo, arigato gozaimasu, and to the Sim Works fam, thank you so much for the trip of a lifetime.
